what: JBT Marel makes food processing equipment. It builds the machines that cut, portion, cook, freeze, inspect and package food in industrial plants, with particular strength in poultry, meat, fish and beverages. It was formed by combining the American company JBT with the Icelandic firm Marel.
customers: Food processors and protein producers worldwide, plus the aftermarket of those same customers needing parts, service and upgrades on installed machines.
money: Processing lines and machinery for protein, beverage and prepared food plants.
Spares, maintenance, upgrades and service contracts on the installed base.
moat: Food processing lines run continuously and a stoppage is expensive, so customers buy parts and service from the original manufacturer rather than risk a cheaper alternative. That installed base generates recurring, high-margin revenue for decades. The JBT and Marel combination also means a processor can now buy a whole line from one supplier instead of integrating several, which is genuinely valuable in plant design.
risks: Reported figures are hard to read across the merger: revenue jumps from $1.7B in 2024 to $3.8B in 2025, and the last fiscal year showed a net loss of $50.5M while the trailing twelve months show $196.5M of profit.
The shares trade at about 32.6 times earnings, which assumes merger synergies arrive largely as promised.
Debt of $2.0B against $167.9M of cash was taken on for the combination, and integrating two engineering companies across continents is slow work.
Equipment orders are capital decisions for food processors and get deferred when protein margins are thin.
Eight analysts average a $160.13 target against $122.40, which implies the market is more sceptical about the integration than the analysts are.
opportunities: The aftermarket is about 40% of revenue, recurring and far more profitable than equipment, and it grows with every machine installed.
Free cash flow of $327.1M exceeds net income, which suggests the underlying cash generation is better than the merger-distorted earnings line.
Automation in food plants is driven by labour scarcity, which is a structural rather than cyclical force: processors automate because they cannot hire.
Combining the two product ranges allows whole-line sales and cross-selling into each company’s installed base, which is the clearest source of synergy.
watch: Aftermarket revenue growth and the integration milestones. The equipment cycle will do what it does; the recurring service base and the merger synergies are what decide whether 32 times earnings was a sensible price.
view: Merged companies are difficult to analyse for two or three years, and JBT Marel is in exactly that fog. Revenue jumped from $1.7 billion to $3.8 billion, the last fiscal year reported a $50 million loss, and the trailing twelve months show $197 million of profit. None of those figures describes the underlying business; they describe accounting for a combination. The useful work here is to look past them at the two things that actually determine the outcome: the quality of the aftermarket base and whether the integration delivers.

The aftermarket is the reason to be interested at all. About 40% of revenue is parts, service and upgrades on machines already installed in food plants, and that revenue is recurring, high margin and almost immune to the equipment cycle. A poultry processor running a line twenty hours a day does not shop around for a cheaper spare part; the cost of a stoppage dwarfs the saving. That installed base has been accumulating for decades at both companies and it grows every time a new line is sold. If you are paying 32 times earnings for a capital equipment maker, this is the part that has to justify it, and it partly does.

The integration case is more interesting than most merger rationales because it is about what the customer buys rather than about cost. Food processors have historically had to assemble a line from several suppliers and make the pieces talk to each other. JBT and Marel together can sell the whole line, which simplifies the plant design and gives the combined company a claim on more of each project. That is a genuine commercial synergy rather than a headcount one. Set against it: these are two engineering cultures on different continents, the debt is $2.0 billion against $168 million of cash, and food equipment orders get deferred the moment protein margins compress.

What I take from the price is that the market is less convinced than the analysts. Eight of them average $160 against a $122 share price, roughly 31% up, while the stock trades where it does. That spread usually means the market is discounting execution risk the analysts are modelling away. I think the market is being appropriately cautious and the business is genuinely good: labour scarcity forces food plants to automate whether or not they feel like spending, and the service base compounds regardless. I would want the integration milestones confirmed and free cash flow holding above reported earnings — which it currently does, at $327 million — before paying up. This is one to underwrite on the aftermarket, not on the order book.
bull: Whole-line selling into both installed bases delivers real commercial synergy while the 40% aftermarket compounds, and cash flow proves better than the merger-distorted earnings.
bear: Integration across two continents drags, protein processors defer capital projects, and 32 times earnings with $2.0 billion of debt meets a deferred equipment cycle.
